content.title: I vote for rejection because this paper has not grasped multiple underlying studies, lacks novelty, and brings small performance improvement.
content.review:
**Summary**

The paper delivers a KD-like method that could yield a better performance metric (e.g., R@1) when the embedding dimension is small. The method, S2SD, brings about +3.5%p (CUB200) and +4.5%p (CARS) performance boost for the R@1 metric.

**Strong points**

- Although additional computing resources required to use the proposed method are not described in the main text and supplementary, additional projections ($g$s) of S2SD lead to performance gains even with small computing resources, presumably.
- This paper has verified the proposed method through a new deep metric learning benchmark presented in academia recently [1], making the result excels in terms of fairness.

**Weak points**

- To say that its method is KD-like is because its teacher network also updates its parameter during the training, and such technique is already well established in the term of *mutual learning* [2]. There is a terminological problem that arises because of this: if the teacher model is also trained with the student, then neither model can be called a "teacher" or "student". Totally omitting the literature related to mutual learning acts as one of the major weaknesses of the paper.
- Very similar work has been published in ECCV 2020 workshop [3]. [3] also brings several auxiliary models to distill their knowledge to each other using in-batch *relational KD* as S2SD does, yet reports better performance than S2SD. Moreover, [3] experimented with more diverse cases such as heterogenous backbones (using both Resnet-50 and BN-inception) or the scalability of the number of models participating in training, showcasing a various aspect of when mutual learning meets deep metric learning, which is rarely covered in this paper.

**Recommendation**

I vote for rejection because this paper has not grasped multiple underlying studies, lacks novelty, and brings small performance improvement.

[1] Roth, Karsten, et al. "Revisiting training strategies and generalization performance in deep metric learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.08473 (2020).  
[2] Zhang, Ying, et al. "Deep mutual learning." Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2018.   
[3] Park, Wonpyo, et al. "Diversified Mutual Learning for Deep Metric Learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2009.04170 (2020).
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3 (1/2)
content.comment:
Before we address each point of concern, we directly address statements made in the review title and summary.

**1. “ Title: (...) brings small performance improvements.”**

We demonstrate that applying S2SD to existing standard state-of-the-art objectives (as studied in [1] and mentioned in Table 1) yields significant performance improvements under fair comparison. S2SD boosts the best performing objectives from [1] by margins close to, or larger than, those seen between best and worst performing objectives studied in [1], which covers DML publications spanning multiple years. To the best of our knowledge, there is no work that achieves comparable performance improvements under the same computational setting and training setup. Further, S2SD could boost the performance of several DML objectives to reach much more complex, orthogonal approaches to DML using e.g. self-supervised learning [b] or feature mining [a].

**2. “ Summary: (...)  that could yield a better performance metric (e.g., R@1) when the embedding dimension is small.”**

This characterization of embedding dimensions as “small” incorrectly interprets these results. Our evaluation setting is more thorough than many setups in DML literature. Our method is tested on nearly every default embedding dimensionality used across DML literature, namely 128/512 on ResNet-50 and 512 on Inception-style architectures. In each case performance is consistently improved and, in most cases, the improvement is very significant. As such, we believe the statement that S2SD "could" boost the performance as not representing our experimental results well. 
We believe that the reviewer may have misinterpreted Figure 3B, where we *additionally* study the benefit of S2SD on embedding dimensions much smaller than the default ones, and for which we find an *even higher* boost in performance. 

**3. “ Although additional computing resources required (...) are not described.”**
 
We note additional computing resources required in Section 5.1 (last sentence); briefly, our method adds at most 5% walltime increase with the most complex setup using multiple, distinct, embedding branches.

**4. “ There is a terminological problem that arises because of this: if the teacher model is also trained with the student, then neither model can be called a "teacher" or "student".”**

We call the additional projections from the shared backbone "teachers" because they operate on a higher embedding dimensionality. This is an intrinsic advantage they have over the lower-dimensional "student" embedding space. Given this prior advantage, “teacher” embedding spaces can naturally learn more complex context, which can then be distilled down to the student. As the direction of distillation also only occurs from high-dimensional teacher to lower-dimensional student, we adopt the knowledge distillation language. The terminological setup resembles [e], with additional teacher components during training time denoted as teacher(s) performing self-distillation to student(s). As such, we believe the teacher-student & distillation terminology used in this submission to be valid.

**5. “ Totally omitting the literature related to mutual learning acts as one of the major weaknesses of the paper.”**

We have **updated the draft** to note that mutual learning can be used as an additional form of extension applicable to DML. 

We do not perform mutual learning as done in [2], as the stream of "distilled knowledge" only goes from the high-dimensional teacher embedding spaces to the lower-dimensional student. Our work has no "mutual" aspect; our approach is more similar to a multi-headed approach from [a] or [b], but cheaper and more effective. We emphasize that unlike the standard mutual learning setting, S2SD *does not* require two (or more) separate, large-scale networks that each require a full training process. Instead we require a few additional fully-connected layers that come at very little additional cost.



See next post for continuation.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3 (2/2)
content.comment:
**6. “ Very similar to ECCV workshop work [3]. “**
We thank the reviewer for pointing us to additional resources. The mentioned work was posted to arXiv very close to the ICLR deadline and, as such, we were not aware of it. Given the lack of peer review and timing of the work, we cannot include a full evaluation in our draft, but address the remarks made about similarity for completeness.

Our work has limited similarity with [3]. Specifically, [3] trains *multiple, separate* networks on differently augmented variants of a mini-batch, and then, in essence, does Mutual learning as in [2] with a mutual KL-Distillation objective.

On the contrary, our work:
* Leverages the fact that knowledge distillation of similarities is agnostic to the dimensionality of the embeddings space operated on, and as such, provides a novel extension to DML by incorporating high-dimensional feature relations to boost generalization performance at very little additional cost, which, to the best of our knowledge, has not been done before.
* Achieves this by using several cheap, fully-connected embedding maps operating on the *same* large network backbone.
* Applies directed and *not* mutual knowledge distillation from high-dimensional teachers to low-dimensional students, as mutual learning would strictly go against the fundamental motivation.

Furthermore, we wish to note that the high performance in [3] can further be attributed to:
* Larger input images (which can boost performance by several percent, see e.g [c, d]),
* Mutual learning using 4 large backbone networks,
* No reported standard deviations.

We therefore believe that:
* Under fair comparison, our method likely matches or even outperforms theirs. Indeed, when looking at Tab. 2, that is already the case for their ResNet-50 baseline.
* Our approach requires much less training time and, as such, has much better scalability to larger datasets.
* _And the final key aspect_: S2SD is *orthogonal* to this mutual learning approach, as we apply a self-distillation-like approach to a single network. This means that when combined, performance can likely be increased further.

_We thus argue that S2SD provides a novel and impactful approach to improve DML generalization and ask the reviewer to reconsider his stance regarding the novelty of our work._


**References:**   
[a] Roth, Karsten et al.,  Mic: Mining interclass characteristics for improved metric learning. In Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision, pp. 8000–8009, 2019.   
[b] Milbich, Timo et al.,  Diva: Diverse visual feature aggregation for deep metric learning. 2020a.   
[c] Kim, Sungyeon et al., Proxy anchor loss for deep metric learning, 2020.   
[d] Roth, Karsten, et al. "Revisiting training strategies and generalization performance in deep metric learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.08473 (2020).   
[e] Be your own teacher: Improve the performance of convolutional neural networks via self distillation. CVPR 2019.

content.title: comment
content.comment:
Thanks to the authors for such a detailed response.

1. I must have skipped the sentence on additional computing resources, thank you for letting me know.
2. I admit that your terminology on distillation is valid as the information flows in an acyclic manner. I misunderstood the flow runs in a mutual manner.
3. The method of incorporating high-dimensional feature relations applied to DML itself is not very novel to me; and I am still unsure whether simply applying the method of self-distillation to DML creates additional contributions. That is because the performance boost is almost guaranteed as investigated in [e] when the self-distillation is performed among additional disposable heads attached after the convolutional backbone.
4. The summary of [3] the authors made is mostly correct, **but [3] not uses the mutual KL-distillation objective**. [3] also uses the knowledge distillation of similarities and also is agnostic to the dimensionality of the embedding space. Thus again, combining similarity-based distillation objectives with DML is not novel to me.

The score will be revised taking into account the review I wrote and the four additional points above.

content.title: Response to comment by AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for his response and appreciate that he took the time to go over the somewhat lengthy response!

Some small notes regarding the last two points:

__3.__ To the best of our knowledge, there is no other work that shows that you can use high-dimensional relational distillation as a strong teacher signal in DML to __very significantly__ improve the performance during training and at very little additional cost! 
It also allows for the usage of multiple distinct teachers at negligible cost for a more robust distillation signal. 

We also note that our distillation operates solely on the last network segment, and as such can be regarded as orthogonal to [e], who leverage a different distillation motivation and objective and solely target distillation at different network hierarchies.
 
__4.__ We assumed a mutual objective as the paper verbatim states: “For each model $f^l$, the knowledge is transferred to all other models in the cohort $\{f^k\}_{k\neq l}$” - as training iterates over all $l\in\{1, ..., L\}$ models, this means that the distillation is applied both from $f^l$ to $f^k$ and $f^k$ to $f^l$. This is different to our strictly acyclic setting, which the reviewer correctly pointed out. 

Finally, it is true that their setup is agnostic to higher dimensionalities, as they rely on a relational formalism. But it is exactly the insight that you *can* (and should) use high-dimensional relations for concurrent distillation that is novel and that gives a very high and cheap performance boost! It is also this insight that allows for the performance boost to be so cheap unlike e.g. [3].

Finally, we wish to reiterate that [3] was published to arxiv very close to the ICLR deadline and ask that it should not be considered when giving the final score - see also the reviewer guide (https://iclr.cc/Conferences/2021/ReviewerGuide):
*"We consider papers contemporaneous if they are published within the last two months. That means, since our full paper deadline is Oct 2, if a paper was published on or after Aug 2, 2020, authors are not required to compare their own work to that paper. (...)."*

content.title: Nice work combining metric learning and self-distillation
content.review:
This paper presents a similarity-based self-distillation method to boost the performance of metric learning by distilling the knowledge from high dimensional embeddings. The proposed will not introduce additional computational cost during inference while improving the retrieval performance. The proposed can be served as a general approach to improve low dimension embeddings, which may be useful in real-world applications. Experiments on standard benchmarks show consistent improvement over several popular baseline methods such as MultiSimilarity and Margin.

I think this is a good paper overall with a new and reasonable method and decent experimental results. Considering the high-quality of this paper, I would like to recommend acceptance. The strengths of this paper are:
- The idea of combining metric learning and self-distillation is interesting and new. Compared to previous methods based on standard knowledge distillation, this method is more flexible and lightweight.
- The experiments look convincing. A consistent improvement over baselines is achieved. The proposed self-distillation method can even outperform Teacher-student distillation.
- This paper is well written and easy to follow. 

Although this paper overall is nice, I still have some concerns/suggestions:
-  This paper uses "Simultaneous Similarity-based Self-distillation" as the main contribution. However, the idea of simultaneous self-distillation is not completely new. A line of work on simultaneous self-distillation [r1, r2] should be compared and discussed. The differences should be highlighted to show the real contribution of this work.
- Recent work [r3] shows RP and mAP@R are more reasonable metrics to evaluate embedding performance. It is suggested to add the results under the two new metrics. 

[r1] Be your own teacher: Improve the performance of convolutional neural networks via self distillation. CVPR 2019.

[r2] MetaDistiller: Network Self-Boosting via Meta-Learned Top-Down Distillation. ECCV 2020.

[r3] A Metric Learning Reality Check, ECCV 2020.


--------
final review:

Thanks for your response.

After reading the authors' feedback and other reviews, I still think it is an interesting work with some new technical contributions and decent improvements based on fair comparisons. I think it is a lightweight and generic method to improve various metric learning methods. Therefore, I would like to keep my initial score.

content.title: Deep metric learning (DML) with focus on making a low-dimensional embedding space
content.review:
This paper tackles deep metric learning (DML) with focus on deriving a low-dimensional embedding space. The main idea is to leverage knowledge self-distillation in two aspects: from high-dim embedding space to low-dim embedding space, and from feature space to embedding space. Overall, the idea of using knowledge distillation for compressing the embedding space for DML is valid and stand. The proposed method is evaluated on three image retrieval datasets with a good setup following a recent work from Roth et al 2020(b).


*** Method ***

1) The description	overall is clear but some details are hard to understand. Concretely, how is the feature distillation formulated in Eq (6). In particular, how is the normalised backbone and how it generates normalized feature representation?

2) The method itself is totally based on self-distillation, hence more self-distillation methods in literature should be included, e.g. [a,b]. -- [a] T. Furlanello, Z. C. Lipton, M. Tschannen, L. Itti, and A. Anand- kumar, “Born again neural networks,” ICML, 2018. [b] X. Lan, X. Zhu, and S. Gong, “Self-referenced deep learning,” in Asian conference on computer vision. 2018.

3) How about combine similarity (pairwise relation) based distillation with more common logins based KL loss?


*** Evaluation ***

1) All three datasets selected are not large scale, smaller than 25,000 images. They are clearly not suitable to demonstrate the performance and efficiency of large scale image retrival as the paper aims to solve. I know that the authors mainly followed the previous studies in data selection. However, it is still an issue in general for the gap between the claims and the experimental setup.

2) The setup following Roth et al. 2020b is a good choice, and evaluation basis.

3) A good set of ablation studies have beed done, which is informative. One missing piece is the performance of auxiliary high-dim embedding space.

4) No time complexity analysis across different embedding dimensions.


*** Minor ***
1) Quite a number of references have no publishing venues. 

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

*Final comments*

Thank the authors for detailed response to all the comments including mines. 

After reading the author responses and the comments of all the reviewers, I would keep my overall rating (learn to accept), although  knowledge distillation is not the first time used for metric learning. Most of my concerns are resolved. The authors have also pointed out the main differences with the most related works raised by peer reviewers. Meanwhile, I agree to some degree that the novelty is not so significant as all the components are from existing works. However, the idea of using KD for dimension compression is valid and the model presented in this work is effective. This would provide the community useful contributions in this specific field at least. 

An extra comment. As clarified by the authors in response, the feature space and embedded space are connected by a dimension reduction layer. This type of design is very similar to the projection head in recent contrastive loss based self-supervised feature learning works (e.g. SimCLR, ICML20). It would be interesting to draw this connection in the final version.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
**1. “ (...) some details are hard to understand. Concretely, how is the feature distillation formulated in Eq (6). In particular, how is the normalized backbone and how it generates normalized feature representation?”**

We normalize the output of the penultimate layer; i.e., the “feature” layer preceding the embedding layer ,which performs the dimensionality reduction. As shown in eq. 6 and the text preceding it, we then apply the same distillation objective as noted in eq. 3 on these normalized feature representations. We have **clarified this better in the updated draft**.

**2. “ (...) hence more self-distillation methods in literature should be included (...)”.**

We thank the reviewer for pointing us to these works. We note that we have referenced Furlanello et al. [a] in the submission already as (Furlanello et al., 2018). However, we were not aware of [b] and have **included it in the updated draft**.

**3. “Comparison to common login (logit?) based Knowledge Distillation.”**

We assume the reviewer meant “logit”-based Knowledge Distillation. Because we primarily aim to distill relations in higher-dimensional hyperspherical embedding spaces, we are unsure how classification-based logit KL Distillation loss could be applied in our setting. We are happy to consider this further in future work. 

**4. “Dataset scales are too small.”**

The stanford online products dataset contains 120,000 images of over 20,000 classes, making it a well-sized object recognition dataset, such that reasonable statements on larger scale generalization behaviours can be made.  

However, we wish to highlight that our primary objective is the improvement of the generalization capability of standard DML methods under a fixed embedding dimensionality, mostly regardless of the dataset size at hand. 
Given the non-overlap between training and test classes in either benchmark, these standard benchmarks provide a very strong indication for the claim of notable generalization improvements by using S2SD.

**5. “No time complexity analysis across different embedding dimensions.”**

Table 3 in the supplementary materials contains a time complexity analysis for image retrieval using different embedding dimensions. As can be seen, the boosting of low embedding dimensions can offer notable time savings without loss in generalization performance, at no notable changes in training time (See end of Section 5.1 - the addition in total walltime did not exceed 5% even for the most demanding S2SD setup).

**6. “Number of references with no publishing venues.”**

We cited most works using their respective Arxiv handle, but have **updated the draft** to ensure that, where possible, work is cited with its respective publication venue.

content.title: AnonReviewer4
content.review:
This paper proposes a simultaneous similarity-based self-distillation (S2SD) approach to alleviate the higher retrieval brought by high dimensional embedding. Through S2SD, this paper can achieve higher results on several benchmarks. Overall, I vote rejection at this time given the following considerations:

Pros:
1) The experiments of S2SD seem to effective in several datasets and the experiments detail is very clear to me.
2)  The methodology part is easy to follow, combine 3 types of distillation make sense to me.

Cons:
1) The first concern is about the motivation of this paper.  From the abstract, it seems the motivation is reducing the high dimensional embedding for retrieval task. However, I did not see explicit experiments to discuss the cost of reducing by the proposed method.

2) The proposed combination of distillation is not very novel to me. It combines with relation distillation, self-distillation and feature distillation. These components have been investigated in the literature.

Thanks to the author response. However, the novelty of this paper for me is not good enough to accept in ICLR. As the authors agree on the relational distillation, self-distillation or feature distillation is existing components. Simply leveraging them in a new context without a very strong and clear motivation is not good. I noticed the discussion between the Authors and Reviewers 3 about the novel part.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for his review. 
Before addressing his concerns point by point, we want to provide additional details w.r.t. to the summary made.

**1. “ Summary ”**

We want to note that the summary does not correctly capture our work. To avoid any misunderstandings, we want to reiterate:
Our work aims to leverage the insight that higher-dimensional embedding spaces offer better generalization, but are bound to much higher application cost at test time. To leverage high-dimensional context for generalization without increasing test time cost, we propose S2SD.
(This can be found in the abstract:  “However, generalization capacity is known to scale with the embedding
space dimensionality. Unfortunately, high dimensional embeddings also create
higher retrieval cost for downstream applications.”)
 
In addition, we not only achieve higher, but state-of-the-art results on all relevant DML benchmarks.

**2. “ The first concern is about the motivation of this paper. From the abstract, it seems the motivation is reducing the high dimensional embedding for retrieval task. However, I did not see explicit experiments to discuss the cost of reducing by the proposed method.”**

As also noted in the abstract, we wish to leverage the fact that "generalization capacity is known to scale with the embedding space dimensionality".
As such, S2SD is to be seen as an *extension* to existing DML methods that makes use of higher-dimensional context to improve the generalization of default DML settings.
Thus, we do not specifically include experiments targeting the cost reduction aspect.
However, Section 5.3 does show that S2SD significantly boosts lower-dimensional embedding spaces to match the performance of much higher dimensional embedding spaces, as such naturally allowing for significant reduction of retrieval cost at test time without losing performance.

**3. “The proposed combination of distillation is not very novel to me. It combines with relation distillation, self-distillation and feature distillation. These components have been investigated in the literature.”**

This statement is unfortunately very generic and misses any references to work that may be similar to ours, and simply refers to the pre-existence of various distillation concepts. Thus, we would ask if the reviewer could specify his concerns.
 
To take some points away, we want to reiterate that we do not assume to have introduced relational distillation, self-distillation or feature distillation. The novelty of our work lies instead in the fact that we leverage relation distillation to be able to incorporate high-dimensional context for generalization in Deep Metric Learning and to naturally address the embedding bottleneck encountered when mapping to lower-dimensional embedding spaces during training.
In doing so, we significantly improve generalization performance and achieve state-of-the-art with little finetuning or additional cost, beating out much more complex methods using e.g. concurrent self-supervised learning [1].
This is especially significant as nearly all other DML objectives experience strong performance saturation [2, 3].
We exemplary also refer to e.g. [4], which proposes self-distillation as a method of improvement for few-shot learning without having invented self-distillation.

**References:**   
[1] Milbich, Timo et al.,  Diva: Diverse visual feature aggregation for deep metric learning. 2020a.   
[2] Roth, Karsten, et al. "Revisiting training strategies and generalization performance in deep metric learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.08473 (2020).   
[3] A Metric Learning Reality Check, ECCV 2020.   
[4] Yonglong Tian, Yue Wang, Dilip Krishnan, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, and Phillip Isola. Rethinking few-shot image classification: a good embedding is all you need?, 2020.

content.title: Overall Comments
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their work, and positive comments on the strength of our results, methodological novelty, thorough experimentation, and clear writing. 
We have uploaded a new draft incorporating all suggested changes.
In the remainder of the response, we denote places which warranted draft corrections with bolded text. 
Finally, we have two general clarifications.

**1.** First, improvements gained with S2SD are very significant - under fair comparison, improvements of best-performing methods with S2SD are larger than the improvements gained by different objectives proposed over the three last years in comparison studies done in [1].

**2.** Second, S2SD allows standard Deep Metric Learning (DML) objectives to match, or substantially beat, performance of much more complex approaches that use self-supervised learning, label-mining or reinforcement learning [2, 3, 4], without a change in training “wall time”.

**References:**   
[1] Roth, Karsten, et al. "Revisiting training strategies and generalization performance in deep metric learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.08473 (2020).   
[2] Milbich, Timo et al.,  Diva: Diverse visual feature aggregation for deep metric learning. 2020a.   
[3] Sanakoyeu, Artsiom et al., Divide and conquer the embedding space for metric learning. In The IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 2019.   
[4] Roth, Karsten et al., Pads: Policy-adapted sampling for visual similarity learning. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), June 2020a.
